title: How to Maximize Social Security Benefits as a Married Couple
description: The 'Split Strategy' and survivor benefit optimization.
content:
For married couples, Social Security is not just two separate checks; it is a joint asset that can be optimized. The difference between a 'Standard Claim' (both at 62) and an 'Optimized Claim' (Split Strategy) can be over $250,000 in lifetime income. The key is understanding how spousal benefits work and prioritizing the 'Survivor Benefit'—ensuring that when one spouse dies, the survivor is left with the highest possible monthly income.

Key Takeaways

  • The Survivor Rule: When one spouse dies, the lower Social Security check disappears. The survivor keeps the higher of the two checks. Therefore, the goal is to maximize the higher earner's record.
  • The 'Split Strategy': The lower earner claims early (62) to generate cash flow now. The higher earner delays until 70 to max out the benefit. This gives you income today and insurance for tomorrow.
  • Spousal Benefit Floor: A spouse is guaranteed at least 50% of the higher earner's Full Retirement Age benefit (if claimed at FRA), even if they never worked. You get the higher of your own benefit or the spousal benefit.
  • The 8% Guarantee: For every year the high earner delays past full retirement age (up to 70), the benefit grows 8%. This is the best inflation-adjusted annuity money can buy.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Social Security claiming strategies used to be more complex ('File and Suspend'), but rules changed in 2015. The current best strategy focuses almost entirely on delaying the high earner's claim to age 70 to protect the surviving spouse against longevity risk.

The $200,000 Decision

Scenario: Husband earns more. Wife earns less. Both are 62.

Option A: Both Claim at 62 (The Mistake)

Husband gets $2,000/mo. Wife gets $1,000/mo.
Total Household: $3,000/mo.
Risk: If Husband dies at 75, Wife is left with only his $2,000 check. Her income drops by 33% while expenses stay high.

Option B: The Split (Optimized)

Wife claims at 62 ($1,000/mo).
Husband waits until 70. His benefit grows to $3,500/mo.
Total Household (at 70): $4,500/mo.
Protection: If Husband dies at 75, Wife inherits his $3,500 check. She is financially secure for life.

The Cost: You must fund the gap years (62-70) from your 401(k). This 'spending down' of assets is worth it to buy the higher guaranteed government paycheck.

Execution Checklist

  1. Identify the High Earner: Look at your SSA.gov statements. Who has the higher Primary Insurance Amount (PIA)? That person is the 'Designated Delayer'.
  2. Bridge Fund: Calculate how much portfolio cash you need to cover expenses while the high earner waits to 70. Set this money aside in a 'Bridge Bucket'.
  3. Health Assessment: If the high earner has a short life expectancy, delaying might not make sense unless the goal is to leave the max benefit to a healthy younger spouse.
  4. Tax Torpedo Defense: While waiting to 70, do Roth Conversions. Your income is artificially low (only one SS check), so you can convert IRA to Roth at a low tax rate.

Frequently Asked Questions

What if we are divorced?

If you were married 10+ years and haven't remarried, you can claim benefits on your ex-spouse's record. It works exactly like spousal benefits and doesn't affect them.

Can I suspend my benefit?

Yes. If you claimed at 62 and regret it, once you reach Full Retirement Age (67), you can 'Suspend' benefits to let them grow 8%/year until 70.

Do both get the delay credits?

Yes, but Spousal Benefits do not earn delay credits past Full Retirement Age. Only the worker's own benefit grows to 70. Spousal benefits max out at 67.
